extracted.intended_audience: Supreme Court Justices/clerks, federal judges, and patent litigators (respondents' counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: A respondent's brief opposing a petition for certiorari concerning patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101, arguing why the petition should be denied and explaining the applicable legal standards and case law. Focuses on Alice/Mayo step-one-and-two analysis, procedural posture (Rule 12(b)(6)), and certiorari standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-step test for §101
rubrics_metrics.description: This Court's two-step test: (1) determine whether the patent claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., an abstract idea); (2) if so, decide whether the claims contain an inventive concept sufficient to transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Alice, 573 U.S. at 217-18; if claims are directed to an ineligible concept at step one, the court proceeds to step two to look for an inventive concept. The brief emphasizes this framework as the controlling inquiry for patent eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 'directed to' inquiry — focus and permissible use of specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Step one asks whether claims are 'directed to' an excluded concept and focuses on the character of the claims 'as a whole' — courts should focus on claim language itself but may use the specification to illuminate what the claims are directed to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specification may be useful to understand 'the problem facing the inventor' and 'what the patent describes as the invention.' Looking to the specification is consistent with Alice and prior Supreme Court decisions (Parker, Adams). However, courts must avoid oversimplifying claims and must not import improper Section 112 enablement considerations into the §101 directed-to analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption risk is central to step one
rubrics_metrics.description: Step one is 'concerned with the risk that a claim will pre-empt others from using an abstract idea' regardless of its implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider whether claim scope would preempt use of an abstract idea; step-one analysis is a stage-one filter to identify claims that essentially monopolize fundamental tools of science and technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical or machine implementation does not automatically make an abstract idea patent eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing an abstract idea on a physical machine or computer does not necessarily render an otherwise ineligible claim eligible; focusing only on the physical aspects would 'make the determination of patent eligibility depend simply on the draftsman's art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Alice, 573 U.S. at 222-24. Claims cannot be rescued solely by reciting generic hardware (e.g., receiver, display, processor) unless there is a particular inventive application or improvement in how the components operate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draftsman's art and Bilski limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The prohibition against patenting abstract ideas cannot be avoided by limiting the ineligible concept to a particular technological environment or by adding insignificant post-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Bilski v. Kappos, 561 U.S. 593, 610 (2010). Merely labeling components (e.g., 'wirelessly coupled') or adding generic physical descriptors (submersible, heat resistant) does not make a claim patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that state a goal without specifying a solution are patent-ineligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that identify a goal to be achieved but do not recite a particular way of achieving it (i.e., no solution) are ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative example: claims like 'illuminating dark rooms by any efficacious means' identify a goal but fail to recite a process for achieving it. The government brief in American Axle is cited for the proposition that claims stating only a goal are ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents directed to analyzing/transmitting/displaying information are frequently ineligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents whose claims are directed to obtaining, analyzing, transmitting, or displaying information (e.g., providing information related to media content) have been consistently held to be abstract ideas and therefore ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Elec. Power Grp., LLC v. Alstom S.A., CyberSource Corp. v. Retail Decisions, Inc., and other Federal Circuit precedent. The brief analogizes the asserted patents to a 'TV Guide'—providing information in conjunction with content is an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 101 is separate from Section 112 (enablement) analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent eligibility under §101 is a distinct inquiry from the enablement and other requirements of §112; §112 considerations should not be folded into §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This brief emphasizes that no party argues for importing §112 into §101 and notes prior Supreme Court guidance that eligibility and enablement are separate inquiries. Nevertheless, specification may be used to illuminate the invention without performing an enablement analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate posture for deciding §101 at Rule 12(b)(6) stage
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court may resolve §101 at the pleadings stage under Rule 12(b)(6) when there are no factual allegations that, taken as true, prevent resolving the eligibility question as a matter of law; subsidiary factual questions may inform the determination but dismissal is inappropriate if plausible allegations preclude resolution as a matter of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts should dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6) only when the record and alleged facts permit resolving eligibility without factual development; courts must not make improper factual findings or resolve disputed facts at the pleadings stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement-style analysis should not be used to improperly disregard claim components
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should not engage in a quasi-enablement or §112-style analysis to disregard concrete claim components when determining what the claim is 'directed to' under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticized practice: treating lack of specification detail as a basis to ignore recited structural components. The brief argues the district court did not do this, but recognizes the line must be observed: specification may illuminate claim focus, but not be used as an enablement substitute to rewrite claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recitation of tangible components is immaterial if the claim is directed to an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere fact that patent claims recite tangible components does not render a claim patent-eligible when the claim's focus is an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Alice: allowing eligibility simply because claims recite physical components would permit claiming any principle via draftsman's art. Courts must look to whether the claimed combination yields a particular inventive manner of performing the abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'law of nature' and 'abstract idea' analyses (American Axle context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different §101 doctrines apply: American Axle concerns the law-of-nature exception (and manufacturing/natural-law issues), while many §101 cases (including this one) concern the abstract-idea exception; the analytic issues and precedential value differ between such cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate American Axle's law-of-nature considerations with abstract-idea cases; the posture and factual record (e.g., summary judgment with claim construction and experts vs. 12(b)(6) dismissal) also matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedential and procedural rules for appellate disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Circuit Rule 36 permits summary affirmance without opinion when an opinion would have no precedential value; certiorari is granted only for compelling reasons (Sup. Ct. R.10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A unanimous or summary affirmance below, and denial of rehearing without written opinion, weigh against granting certiorari; routine misapplication-of-law complaints are rarely sufficient grounds for Supreme Court review.
